summary: States use cases and requirements for SIP-based media recording. Call centers and financial trading floors often must record calls for regulatory reasons or quality control, typically by sending a copy of the media to a recording device. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some businesses must keep recordings of phone calls. This describes why and what an internet-phone system needs in order to send a copy of each call to a recorder.

questions: what is a session recording server
what is the difference between a communication session and a recording session
subtitle: Twelve recording scenarios and 31 requirements for copying SIP call media to a recorder.

tldr.problem: Call centers and financial trading floors often must record calls for regulatory, compliance or quality reasons, but there is no standard way to control delivery of the media to a recording device.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6341 defines a Session Recording Client that sends a copy of the call media and metadata to a Session Recording Server over its own SIP session, and lists 12 use cases and 31 numbered requirements for the extensions needed.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document only. It specifies no protocol itself, and it covers active recording where the client streams media on purpose.

today: RFC 6341 is an Informational RFC with no recorded obsoleting or updating RFC in the unit metadata. It states requirements only and does not define the protocol that meets them.

sections.title: Why Sessions Get Recorded
sections.content:
Session recording is a critical requirement in businesses where voice is used for commerce and customer support. Financial trading floors typically must record all calls, for dispute resolution and compliance. Call centers typically record only a subset, for quality control or business analytics, and their calls must not fail whatever the state of the recording device.

Privacy is called paramount. In many jurisdictions participants have a right to know a session is or might be recorded, and to opt out by ending the call or demanding it not be recorded. Use cases where users are not informed are out of scope, and so is lawful intercept. The document also stresses that a standard solution must support optionality and flexibility, or proprietary solutions will keep spreading in cheaper markets.
sections.plainLanguage: Banks and help desks sometimes have to keep recordings of calls. Everyone on the call has a right to be told, so the system must allow that.

sections.title: The Recording Roles
sections.content:
The Session Recording Client (SRC) is a SIP user agent that is the source of the recorded media. It is a logical function, and in practice could be a SIP phone, a media gateway, a session border controller, or a media server with an application server. The Session Recording Server (SRS) is a SIP user agent that is the sink of the recorded media and metadata, typically a multi-port device that receives from many sources at once.

The call being recorded is the Communication Session (CS). The SIP session between the SRC and SRS that carries the copy is the Recording Session (RS). Metadata describes the recorded media and the CS, so archives can be searched later and played back with correct synchronization.

Only active recording is in scope, where the SRC purposely streams media to an SRS. Passive recording, where a device picks up media directly from the network, is outside the scope. Any RTP media can be recorded, including voice, DTMF, video and text.
sections.plainLanguage: One side makes a copy of the call and sends it; the other side collects and files it. The call and the copy are two separate connections.

sections.title: Twelve Use Cases
sections.content:
Section 4 lists 12 use cases. The first four are about when a Recording Session exists relative to calls: full-time recording with one RS per CS, selective recording of only some calls, starting and stopping an RS during a call (manually by a phone button or automatically by an application), and persistent recording where one RS spans many calls.

Persistent recording avoids media clipping that can occur due to delays in RS establishment, and periods with no call must be reproduced on playback, for example by recording silence or marking them with metadata. A trading-floor turret may even mix several concurrent calls into one RS.

The rest cover real-time controls such as pause and resume (for example, not recording a caller speaking a credit card number for PCI compliance), IVR recording, mobile and home-based workers, centralized recording for sites that may number up to thousands of small branches, linked calls such as an agent consulting a supervisor, high availability, multi-channel multimedia recording, and real-time media processing such as speech analytics.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you record every call, sometimes just a few, and sometimes you leave the recorder running all day. There are twelve situations like these to plan for.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
Section 5 lists 31 requirements, REQ-001 to REQ-031, all phrased with MUST or MUST NOT. They fall into a few groups:

  • Session control: use SIP to establish, maintain and terminate Recording Sessions; record all calls, selected calls, or selected parts of calls; support pause, resume and stop.
  • Media: record voice, DTMF, video and text; deliver mixed audio from several calls or parties, and multiple streams for one call or of the same media type, such as unmixed audio per participant.
  • No impact on the call: record without clipping media at the start and without delaying or degrading the call (REQ-005); do not prevent high-availability deployments.
  • Metadata and timing: give the SRS metadata about the call, let it correlate recorded media with participants, send metadata incrementally, and support synchronization of streams and metadata and relating controls to wall clock time.
  • User awareness: let a recording-aware user agent request that a call be recorded or not, or start, pause, resume or stop recording, subject to policy and with notification of the outcome; do not block tones or announcements; indicate whether recording is taking place.
  • Protection: mutual authentication of SRC and SRS, integrity of media and metadata, and confidentiality of metadata and the Recording Session.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper has a checklist of 31 things a recording system must be able to do, such as start, stop, pause, tell people, and keep the copy safe.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Notification rules vary widely by jurisdiction. Not every user will be allowed to stop a recording, though any user can leave the call. Callers to a call center usually have to ask the agent not to record, and if that fails or they do not trust the agent, the only option is generally to end the call. What happens to a recording afterwards (who can access it, for what purpose, how long it is kept) is treated as domain policy, and the document sets no requirement for users to dictate that policy.

On security, both signaling and media of the Recording Session need authentication and eavesdropping protection. The security level of a Recording Session need not match that of the call: an SRS in a public cloud might need stronger protection than the call, for instance. A malicious or corrupt SRC can tamper with media and metadata, and ways to ensure the correctness of what an SRC emits are outside the scope of this work.
sections.plainLanguage: People should be told when they are recorded, and the copy has to be kept private and safe. The rules about who may listen later belong to the company doing the recording.

viz.caption: THE FOUR TERMS THE RFC DEFINES

items.title: SRC
items.text: Session Recording Client: the SIP user agent that is the source of recorded media.

items.title: SRS
items.text: Session Recording Server: the SIP user agent that is the sink of recorded media and metadata.

items.title: CS
items.text: Communication Session: the call between participants that is the subject of recording.

items.title: RS
items.text: Recording Session: the SIP session between an SRC and an SRS that records a CS.
